analysis.one_liner: Sends families $300–$360 per child every month as a fully refundable tax credit.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 9, 2025 with 44 cosponsors — every Senate Democrat and both independents — and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has seen no markup, hearing, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the current $2,000 child tax credit with a larger, fully refundable monthly payment: $300 a month for each child age 6 or older, $360 a month for each child under 6, and $2,400 in a newborn's first month. Because the credit is fully refundable, the lowest-income families would get the full amount, which the current credit does not allow. It would also create a $500 credit for other dependents and extend the benefit to families in Puerto Rico and the other territories. The bill contains no provisions to raise revenue to cover its cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 18, especially low- and middle-income ones. Under current law the child tax credit is not fully refundable, so many low-income families get a reduced amount or nothing; this bill would pay every eligible family the full monthly amount. Payments arrive monthly rather than once a year at tax time, and the amount grows with inflation.

how_it_helps.text: Pays $300 per month for each child age 6 or older and $360 per month for each child under 6, with $2,400 in the first month of a child's life [S2].
Makes the credit fully refundable, so families with little or no income tax liability receive the full amount — under the current credit, many low-income families cannot [S2].
Delivers the credit monthly in advance, so families get the money throughout the year instead of a lump sum at tax time [S2].
Phases the credit down only above $150,000 for couples and $112,500 for single filers, reaching a floor of $166.67 per month, with a second phase-out above $400,000 for couples [S2].
Adds a $500 annual credit for non-child dependents such as elderly or disabled relatives [S2].
Extends the benefit to residents of Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories, who are largely excluded from the current credit [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The bill includes no taxes or offsets to pay for the new, larger credit, so the cost is added to the federal deficit and borne by taxpayers generally, including future ones. Families above the income thresholds keep a reduced benefit rather than the full amount, and families whose children lack a taxpayer identification number cannot claim the credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no revenue offsets: it enlarges a major federal benefit entirely by adding to the deficit, a cost the text does not address [S2].

A child must have a taxpayer identification number issued by the return due date for the family to claim the credit, which can exclude some otherwise-eligible children, such as those whose documentation is delayed [S2].

Monthly advance payments require the IRS to estimate eligibility from older tax data; when income rises or custody changes during the year, families can receive too much and owe it back, as happened with the 2021 advance child payments (general knowledge about how advance payment mechanisms work).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to families with children is large and direct: more money per child, delivered monthly, and finally reaching the lowest-income families the current credit leaves out. The main weakness is that the bill does not pay for itself, so its cost lands on the deficit — an honest supporter would need to pair it with revenue or accept that trade. The anti-fraud restrictions and ID requirements are real but standard for refundable credits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where no markup, hearing, or vote has ever been scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the American Family Act on April 9, 2025 with 44 cosponsors: 42 of the 45 Senate Democrats and both independents [S3].
No Republican senator cosponsored the bill [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, and the action history shows nothing since — no markup, no hearing, no vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet: the current $2,000 child tax credit remains in place. If the bill dies in committee, families with children never see the larger benefit, while the federal deficit is untouched and households above the phase-out thresholds keep current-law treatment.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Families keep the smaller credit; deficit untouched

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 44 cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, whose referral landed in his committee.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a committee markup on the bill; it has sat in his committee since April 2025 with no further action.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors are Democrats or independents (42 of 45 Senate Democrats, 2 of 2 independents); not a single Republican senator has signed on.

industries.note: The bill phases the credit down for couples earning over $150,000 and further for those over $400,000, leaving them at or near the current-law benefit instead of the full new amount. No employer or industry is materially affected by this bill; its concentrated costs fall on upper-income families and the federal deficit, which all taxpayers share.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, no Republican cosponsors, and no revenue offsets in the bill, it is unlikely to get a Finance Committee markup or a floor vote this Congress. Bennet has introduced versions of this bill in several prior Congresses and each died in committee without a vote.
